title: Florence — The Competition That Began the Renaissance
teaser: Two young goldsmiths compete to cast bronze doors for the Florence Baptistery. One loses and invents a new architecture. In Paris, Chaucer's pilgrims fall silent forever. In Avignon and Rome, rival popes excommunicate each other. The medieval world cracks open.

art.label: Art
art.content: In 1401, Florence's wool merchants guild announces a competition for new bronze doors on the Baptistery of San Giovanni. Seven sculptors submit trial panels depicting the Sacrifice of Isaac. The finalists: Lorenzo Ghiberti, twenty-three, elegant and technically flawless, and Filippo Brunelleschi, twenty-four, dramatic and classical. The judges declare a tie. Ghiberti claims victory; Brunelleschi refuses to collaborate and withdraws. This rivalry defines the Early Renaissance: Ghiberti will spend twenty-one years on the doors, then create the Gates of Paradise. Brunelleschi, rejected, abandons sculpture entirely and turns to architecture — where he will crown Florence with a dome that defies all precedent. Meanwhile, the International Gothic style still dominates Europe's courts: the Limbourg brothers illuminate manuscripts for the Duke of Berry, all gold leaf and courtly elegance. Florence is choosing something different: competition, classical revival, individual genius.

lit.label: Literature
lit.content: On 25 October 1400, Geoffrey Chaucer dies in London, his Canterbury Tales unfinished. Twenty-four of one hundred twenty planned tales complete — pilgrims frozen mid-journey, their storytelling contest eternally suspended. Yet those fragments revolutionize English literature: the vernacular elevated to art, character emerging from type, irony tempering piety. In Paris, Christine de Pizan — widow, professional writer, the first woman in Europe to earn her living by the pen — is composing works that defend women against the misogyny of Le Roman de la Rose. Her Book of the City of Ladies (1405) will build an allegorical city from the stories of virtuous women. Two vernaculars, two nations, two transformations of who can write and what writing can do.

phil.label: Philosophy
phil.content: In Paris, Jean Gerson, Chancellor of the University since 1395, confronts an impossible question: if there are two popes, who has authority to judge between them? His answer transforms political philosophy. Conciliarism argues that a general council of the Church holds authority superior even to the pope — that legitimacy flows from the gathered body, not the singular head. Gerson tempers the nominalism of William of Ockham with mystical theology, arguing that experience and prayer ground knowledge more surely than logical speculation. In Florence, Coluccio Salutati, humanist chancellor, wages a different philosophical war: his Latin letters defending the Florentine Republic are so devastating that Milan's duke says they do more damage than a thousand cavalry. Civic humanism is born — the active life reconciled with philosophical virtue.

hist.label: History
hist.content: The Western Schism has torn Christendom for twenty-three years: Boniface IX reigns in Rome, Benedict XIII in Avignon, each excommunicating the other's followers. Europe's kingdoms choose sides by politics, not theology. In Wales, Owain Glyndŵr declares himself Prince of Wales and launches a rebellion that will burn for fifteen years. But the real storm gathers in the East: Timur (Tamerlane), the Turko-Mongol conqueror, sacks Damascus in 1401, massacres Baghdad's population, builds towers from severed heads. He demands skilled artisans as tribute, draining cities of craftsmen to glorify his capital Samarkand. The Timurid Renaissance flowers atop mountains of skulls.

conn.label: Connections
conn.content: The threads converge in a single question: who decides? In Florence, a committee of thirty-four judges picks between rival artists — competition replacing patronage as the engine of innovation. In Paris, Gerson argues that councils, not popes, can legitimate authority — consent replacing divine right. Salutati's civic humanism insists that virtue requires participation in public life, not retreat from it. Even Chaucer's pilgrims vote on whose tale is best. The old medieval certainties — one Pope, one Emperor, one Truth — are fracturing into pluralism. Florence's baptistery doors don't just depict Isaac's sacrifice; they inaugurate a new covenant: that genius must be tested, authority must be earned, and the future belongs to whoever can persuade the judges.
conn.funFact: Both Brunelleschi's and Ghiberti's competition panels survive in Florence's Bargello Museum — the world's first art historical A/B test, preserved for six centuries.
